items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: The New Frontier
items.summary: Google just announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its second frontier model in about two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. According to Artificial Analysis, Carbon is now #1 on their Intelligence Index at 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. Google says Carbon leads across the whole cyber defense workflow: finding vulnerabilities (SEC-bench Pro 88.2%), proving they can be exploited (ExploitGym 54.8%) and writing the patch (CWE-bench 71.0%). Google also says successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 dropped to 0%. On Arena's Agent leaderboard, Carbon ranks #2 behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 72% lower cost per task, based on Arena's testing. Carbon isn't publicly available yet. It's going to cyber defenders first through Google's Fairwind program, at the same introductory price as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Fun fact: put carbon under enough pressure and you get a diamond. Sources: Gemini 4 Argon video: https://youtu.be/clNh3f97b2Y Google announcement: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/ Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index Arena's results: https://x.com/arena/status/2115495002998751262 Google DeepMind: https://x.com/GoogleDeepMind/status/2115489356437651654 #Gemini4 #GeminiCarbon #GoogleDeepMind #AI #LLM #Shorts

items.title: What the AI Chatbot Leaves Out
items.summary: The chatbot read the whole buffet menu and served you one very nice sandwich. You left full and never found out they served your favorite soup. Researchers at the University of Copenhagen tested 27 chatbots against Google search on 155 topics. They measured how many different claims showed up, and the search results had more. That doesn't mean the chatbots were wrong, and newer ones were getting more varied. Still, a tidy summary can make me feel done before I've heard the other side. For a big decision, I want the usual answer and the argument against it.

items.title: Evolve on Graph now trains your AI model (w/ code)
items.summary: Evolve on Graph (EoG), a new framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning: without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. Looped self-learning. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver’s score variance, keeping questions at the Solver’s capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. items.title: NCM: The End of LLMs? Not So Fast (Local Tests)
items.summary: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) from Stanford’s Hazy Research writes an answer as a rough sketch first and the exact words last, in a handful of passes instead of one pass per token. I ran the released models on a DGX Spark and timed NCM against a same-size word-by-word LLM: it’s up to 4x faster for one request and 4–8x slower at 64 requests. I also trained my own diffusion model, which tied NCM’s 86% on hard Sudoku once it filled the most confident cell first. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14162 Code: https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm Check

items.title: When It Doesn't Matter That It's Slop (Paul Lessard)
items.summary: Paul Lessard on where AI has already replaced people. Translation was a white-collar job that has essentially disappeared, and whether these systems replace people or simply de-skill them hardly matters to the companies using them. Wherever getting it exactly right, or meeting a refined sense of what is good, doesn't matter, it has already happened: when it doesn't matter that it's slop, it's going to be slop. There may be no formal line between where slop is acceptable and where it isn't. That boundary, he argues, is cultural and aesthetic, and that makes it a question of politics.
